lines.text: From a handful of linked university computers to a network in nearly every pocket. This is the story of the internet, the people, protocols and sites that built it.
It starts with the people. Bob Kahn, an American engineer on the ARPANET, believed networks of every kind should be joined by one shared set of rules.
With Vint Cerf, he designed those rules, TCP and IP. Cerf is often called one of the fathers of the internet, and later worked at Google.
And Tim Berners-Lee, a British scientist at CERN, would one day propose the World Wide Web and write its first browser and server.
First, a way to talk down a phone line. The modem turned a computer's signals into sound and back, and later took millions online with a famous screech.
In the mid sixties, Paul Baran and Donald Davies each hit on the same idea: cut data into small packets that travel separately and rejoin at the end.
By 1969, Telnet let you log in to a distant computer and type as if you sat beside it, though everything travelled unencrypted.
That same year CompuServe began, one of the first online services for the public, with forums, email and downloads over dial-up.
Also in 1969, the American defence network ARPANET linked its first computers by packet switching. It would grow into the internet itself.
In 1971 came FTP, a way to move files between computers that is older than TCP and IP, and lasted for decades.
The same year, the first email passed between two different computers, with the at sign in its address. Writing online had begun.
In 1973 Xerox PARC devised Ethernet, a cable that links the computers in a building. It became the standard for local networks.
Then TCP and IP took shape: rules to break data into packets, route them across linked networks and put them back together. The whole internet rests on them.
By the late seventies hobbyists ran bulletin boards from home, computers you dialled to leave messages and swap files. They were the online communities before the web.
In France, Minitel gave households a little terminal for directories, shopping, banking and chat, years before the web arrived.
Meanwhile Usenet spread its newsgroups from server to server, a worldwide discussion where much of internet culture was born.
In 1981 the Hayes Smartmodem set the commands every dial-up modem would understand, connecting home computers to bulletin boards and, later, the internet.
A year later, SMTP set out how email passes from server to server. With changes, it still carries nearly all of it today.
Then AOL arrived. Its free trial discs seemed to be everywhere, and in the nineties they brought millions of households online.
Also in 1983, the Domain Name System became the internet's address book, turning names into the numbers computers use.
In 1985 NSFNET linked American universities and supercomputer centres, and became the backbone of the early internet.
In 1988 IRC brought live group chat in text, organised in channels. It was the internet's chat room for twenty years.
Now the web takes shape. In 1989 Tim Berners-Lee wrote the first version of HTML, the code that describes a page's headings, links and pictures.
Next came HTTP, the rules a browser uses to ask a server for a page. It is still the basis of nearly every site.
In 1991 Gopher, from the University of Minnesota, offered menus of documents and was more popular than the web at first, until licence fees drove people away.
That same year the World Wide Web went public. When CERN made it royalty free in 1993, it spread to everyone.
In 1993 the Mosaic browser showed pictures beside text, and suddenly the web looked like something anyone would want to use.
In 1994 two students turned their list of favourite sites into Yahoo, which became the front page of the internet for the nineties.
Its first product, the Yahoo Directory, sorted websites by hand into categories, and it was how many people found their way around.
Lycos, a search engine from Carnegie Mellon, became one of the best known early portals, bought high at the boom and sold far lower.
Also in 1994 came Netscape Navigator. Its share offering a year later set off the dot-com boom.
From the mid nineties, internet shares soared, even for firms with no profits. When the bubble burst in 2000, many companies went down with it.
One that survived began in 1995 as a bookshop on the web. Amazon grew into the shop that sells nearly everything.
Microsoft answered Netscape with Internet Explorer, given away with Windows. It won the first browser war with about nineteen users in every twenty.
Netscape built JavaScript in 1995 to make pages move and respond. Today it runs in every browser, and on servers too.
Excite, a portal and search engine, was among the busiest sites of the late nineties, until the crash left it a quiet page for years.
And AltaVista searched the full text of the web, fast. For a few years, it was where most people started.
In 1996 the Flash plug-in brought animation, games and video to the web, and would carry YouTube's first videos.
That year engineers also drew up IPv6, a new addressing system for when the old one ran short. Its adoption has been slow.
In 1997 a butler called Jeeves invited you to ask questions in plain English, one of the best known names of the early web.
The same year Google began ranking pages by the links pointing at them. Its answers were better, and the name became a verb.
SixDegrees let you list your friends and see their friends, often called the first social network, but it came before most people were online.
And Wi-Fi cut the cable, letting laptops and later phones connect through a nearby base station. Now it is in nearly every home.
In 1998 the American government took Microsoft to court over bundling its browser with Windows. A breakup was ordered, then overturned, and the case was settled.
Behind the padlock in your browser is TLS, grown from Netscape's SSL, which encrypts payments, passwords and private messages.
In 2000 Baidu launched, and became the main search engine of China, used by hundreds of millions.
In 2001 came an encyclopedia anyone could edit. Wikipedia was expected to fail, and instead became where the world looks things up.
From Netscape's released code grew Firefox, the open browser that broke Internet Explorer's hold in the two thousands.
In 2003 Apple launched Safari. On the iPhone, it would become the second most used browser in the world.
Now social networks take off. Friendster was the first to reach millions, but its pages loaded so slowly that people left.
LinkedIn made a social network for work, where your profile is your CV and your contacts are colleagues.
And Myspace became the biggest network of its day: decorate your page, pick your top eight friends, discover new bands.
Google tried with Orkut in 2004. It never caught on in America, but for years it was the social network of Brazil and India.
That year a site for students at one university began. Facebook would go on to connect about three billion people.
Flickr gave photographers a place to share, and introduced tags and public photo streams before everyone shared pictures.
On Digg, readers voted news stories up or down, until a disliked redesign sent most of them elsewhere.
In 2005 YouTube let anyone post a video and anyone watch it. It is now the second most visited website in the world.
That same year Reddit opened its discussion boards, one for every interest, where votes decide what rises.
Bebo was a hit with young people in Britain, Ireland and Australia, until Facebook drew them away and it went bankrupt.
In 2006 came Twitter, short public messages anyone could pass on. It became where news broke first.
In Russia, VK began that year as a network for students, and grew into the most visited site in the country.
Tumblr followed in 2007, a home for short posts, pictures and the fan communities that gathered around them.
Now the internet moves to the phone. In 2008 Google launched Chrome, which overtook Internet Explorer within four years.
The same year DuckDuckGo promised a search engine that would not track the people who used it.
In 2009 WhatsApp replaced paid text messages with messages over the internet. In many countries it is simply how people talk.
Microsoft launched Bing that year to take on Google, and it has stayed a distant second.
And in 2009 came Bitcoin, money with no bank in the middle, kept track of in a shared public record called the blockchain.
In 2010 Pinterest let people pin pictures to boards, for recipes, crafts, fashion and ideas for the home.
Google Buzz made people's contacts public by default. The outcry was immediate, and it closed a year later.
Mt. Gox handled most of the world's Bitcoin trades for a time, then collapsed when about eight hundred and fifty thousand coins went missing.
Instagram's filters made ordinary phone photos look good. Facebook bought it when it had just thirteen employees.
In 2011 China got WeChat, messages, payments and shopping in one app, used by more than a billion people.
The hidden market Silk Road sold drugs for bitcoin, until the FBI shut it down in 2013.
Google+ was Google's answer to Facebook. Millions were signed up, but few stayed.
Snapchat made pictures vanish after they were seen, and popularised the short-lived Story.
In 2012 Coinbase opened in America as an exchange for buying and selling crypto, and joined the stock market in 2021.
Vine's six-second looping videos lasted only four years, but started a style of short comedy that TikTok later made enormous.
Zoom launched in 2013, and when schools and offices closed in the pandemic, it became part of daily life.
Dogecoin began as a joke with a Shiba Inu dog for a face, and later soared on social media.
NFTs recorded who owned a digital picture. Sales boomed in 2021 and collapsed soon after.
In 2015 Microsoft Edge replaced Internet Explorer, and five years later it was rebuilt on Chrome's open code.
Ethereum went live that summer, a blockchain that runs small programs called smart contracts alongside its currency.
Tether followed, a stablecoin meant to be worth one American dollar each, and the largest of its kind.
Mastodon built a social network from many independent servers, and many people moved there after Twitter was sold.
Founded in 2017, Binance grew into the largest crypto exchange in the world by trading volume.
Now we are always online. TikTok's endless feed of short videos, chosen for you by software, grew faster than any social app before it.
In 2018 reporters revealed that a consulting firm had taken data on millions of Facebook users through a quiz. Inquiries and a large fine followed.
In 2019 the first 5G networks switched on, faster and with room for many connected devices.
That year SpaceX began launching Starlink, thousands of small satellites bringing the internet to remote places and ships.
Bluesky began as a project inside Twitter and grew fast as users left X.
In 2021 El Salvador became the first country to make bitcoin legal money.
In November 2022 the exchange FTX collapsed, and its founder was later convicted of fraud.
That year Elon Musk bought Twitter for forty-four billion dollars, cut most of its staff, and renamed it X.
In 2023 Meta answered with Threads, linked to Instagram, and gained a hundred million sign-ups in a few days.
From one network of a few computers to billions of people online, and the story is still being written.
